title: An earthquake stretched Japan's Akashi Kaikyō Bridge by a metre while it was being built

cover.alt: The Akashi Kaikyō suspension bridge spanning the strait near Kobe, with its two tall towers and long sweeping cables.

body: When the Great Hanshin earthquake struck near Kobe on 17 January 1995, the **Akashi Kaikyō Bridge** was half-built: only its two towers stood. The ground shifted sideways along the fault and carried the towers with it, so the planned central span of 1,990 m had to be increased to **1,991 m**. The bridge opened on 5 April 1998 with the longest suspension span in the world, a title it held until Turkey's 1915 Çanakkale Bridge opened in March 2022. Its towers rise 282.8 m above the sea, its main cables are 112 cm thick and contain about 300,000 km of wire, and it is designed to withstand winds of 286 km/h and earthquakes up to magnitude 8.5.

slides.prompt: The towers were planned 1,990 m apart. After the magnitude 6.9 quake, how far apart were they?
slides.detail: The earthquake moved the towers, the only parts yet built, so the central span had to be increased by 1 m. The design was adapted and construction carried on.
